name: Lorazepam
route_note: Oral or sublingual tablets; IV or IM injection for status epilepticus and sedation; an extended-release capsule exists in the US.
targets: GABA-A receptors (benzodiazepine site, positive allosteric modulator)
owner: generic (many); Bausch Health (Ativan, US), Pfizer (Temesta, some markets)

discovery.note: A 3-hydroxy benzodiazepine developed at Wyeth in the 1960s, closely related to oxazepam.

tagline: High-potency benzodiazepine and a first-line drug for status epilepticus
summary: Lorazepam is a high-potency, intermediate-acting benzodiazepine used for anxiety, insomnia related to anxiety, premedication and as a first-line treatment for status epilepticus. It is metabolised by glucuronidation without active metabolites, which makes it useful in liver disease and in older people.
mechanism: Lorazepam enhances GABA-A receptor function at the benzodiazepine site, increasing chloride channel opening frequency and neuronal inhibition, which produces anxiolytic, sedative, amnesic, anticonvulsant and muscle-relaxant effects.
Compared with diazepam it is less lipophilic, so redistribution out of the brain is slower and anticonvulsant action after IV dosing lasts longer.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Ativan is approved in the US.

history.title: Status epilepticus trial
history.detail: Leppik and colleagues report a double-blind comparison of IV lorazepam and diazepam in status epilepticus (JAMA).

history.title: Pre-hospital trial
history.detail: A NEJM trial shows paramedic-administered lorazepam or diazepam is effective for out-of-hospital status epilepticus.

history.title: Opioid boxed warning
history.detail: The FDA adds a boxed warning on combined use with opioids.

history.title: Class boxed warning
history.detail: The benzodiazepine boxed warning is expanded to abuse, dependence and withdrawal reactions.

history.title: Loreev XR
history.detail: An extended-release once-daily capsule is approved in the US.

pk.metabolism: Hepatic glucuronidation to inactive lorazepam glucuronide (no CYP)

serious: Propylene glycol toxicity with high-dose infusions
safety.boxed_warning: Concomitant use with opioids may cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death. Risks of abuse, misuse and addiction; continued use may lead to clinically significant physical dependence, and abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction may cause life-threatening withdrawal reactions.

facts: The 2001 NEJM pre-hospital trial (Alldredge et al.) is a landmark in out-of-hospital seizure care.
